claim: Hin is a member of the DNA invertase subclass of serine recombinases that are regulated by a remote recombinational enhancer element containing two binding sites for the protein Fis.
source: Hin is a member of the DNA invertase subclass of serine recombinases that are regulated by a remote recombinational enhancer element containing two binding sites for the protein Fis.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the classification and regulation of Hin.

claim: Two Hin dimers bound to specific recombination sites associate with the Fis-bound enhancer by DNA looping where they are remodeled into a synaptic tetramer competent for DNA chemistry and exchange.
source: Two Hin dimers bound to specific recombination sites associate with the Fis-bound enhancer by DNA looping where they are remodeled into a synaptic tetramer competent for DNA chemistry and exchange.
evidence: This statement describes the mechanism of Hin recombination as presented in the abstract.

claim: The flexible beta-hairpin arms of the Fis dimers contact the DNA binding domain of one subunit of each Hin dimer.
source: Here we show that the flexible beta-hairpin arms of the Fis dimers contact the DNA binding domain of one subunit of each Hin dimer.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by crosslinking experiments shown in the results.

claim: These contacts sandwich the Hin dimers to promote remodeling into the tetramer.
source: These contacts sandwich the Hin dimers to promote remodeling into the tetramer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A basic region on the Hin catalytic domain contacts enhancer DNA to complete assembly of the active Hin tetramer.
source: A basic region on the Hin catalytic domain then contacts enhancer DNA to complete assembly of the active Hin tetramer.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by mutagenesis and FeBABE experiments in the results.

claim: Site-specific recombination reactions have evolved as a relatively simple solution to a myriad of biological problems including gene regulation, viral integration, DNA transposition, chromosome segregation, and the programmed creation of genetic diversity.
source: Site-specific recombination reactions have evolved as a relatively simple solution to a myriad of biological problems including gene regulation, viral integration, DNA transposition, chromosome segregation, and the programmed creation of genetic diversity (Craig, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Craig, 2002.

claim: Most site-specific recombinases can be classified into two structurally and mechanistically unrelated groups that are named for the use of either a serine or tyrosine as the active site residue.
source: Most site-specific recombinases can be classified into two structurally and mechanistically unrelated groups that are named for the use of either a serine or tyrosine as the active site residue (Grindley et al., 2006).
evidence: This classification is supported by a citation to Grindley et al., 2006.

claim: The synaptic complexes formed by serine recombinases contain the two recombining DNA segments on the outside of a tetrameric protein core.
source: The synaptic complexes formed by serine recombinases contain the two recombining DNA segments on the outside of a tetrameric protein core (Dhar et al., 2004; Nollmann et al., 2004; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This structural description is supported by multiple citations.

claim: All four DNA strands are cleaved by near simultaneous attack on the DNA backbone by the catalytic serines to form 5′-phosphoserine linkages, thereby generating double-strand breaks at both recombination sites.
source: All four DNA strands are cleaved by near simultaneous attack on the DNA backbone by the catalytic serines to form 5′-phosphoserine linkages, thereby generating double-strand breaks at both recombination sites.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of DNA cleavage by serine recombinases, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: DNA strands are exchanged by a subunit rotation mechanism where one pair of synapsed subunits, together with their covalently-bound DNA strands, rotates 180° relative to the other pair.
source: DNA strands are then exchanged by a subunit rotation mechanism where one pair of synapsed subunits, together with their covalently-bound DNA strands, rotates 180° relative to the other pair (Stark et al., 1989; Dhar et al., 2004, 2009a, 2009b; Li et al., 2005; Bai et al., 2011).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hin inverts a ∼1 kb segment of chromosomal DNA between two 26 bp hix recombination sites in Salmonella enterica.
source: Hin inverts a ∼1 kb segment of chromosomal DNA between two 26 bp hix recombination sites in Salmonella enterica (Zieg et al., 1977; Zieg and Simon, 1980).
evidence: This describes the biological function of Hin and is supported by citations.

claim: Inversion switches the orientation of a promoter, resulting in alternative expression of flagellin genes.
source: Inversion switches the orientation of a promoter, resulting in alternative expression of flagellin genes.
evidence: This describes the biological consequence of Hin-mediated DNA inversion.

claim: Flagellar phase variation is one way that Salmonella evades the host immune system.
source: Flagellar phase variation is one way that Salmonella evades the host immune system.
evidence: This describes the biological significance of flagellar phase variation.

claim: DNA inversion by Hin occurs upon assembly of the invertasome, a tripartite nucleoprotein complex made up of four Hin subunits bound to two hix sites and the recombinational enhancer element.
source: DNA inversion by Hin occurs upon assembly of the invertasome, a tripartite nucleoprotein complex made up of four Hin subunits bound to two hix sites and the recombinational enhancer element (Figure 1A) (Heichman and Johnson, 1990).
evidence: This describes the invertasome structure and is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The enhancer is a 65 bp DNA sequence that has recognition sites for the bacterial nucleoid-associated DNA binding and bending protein Fis on each end.
source: The enhancer is a 65 bp DNA sequence that has recognition sites for the bacterial nucleoid-associated DNA binding and bending protein Fis on each end.
evidence: This describes the structure of the enhancer element.

claim: The hin enhancer is normally positioned about 100 bp from one of the hix sites.
source: Whereas the hin enhancer is normally positioned about 100 bp from one of the hix sites, it can efficiently activate DNA inversion many kb away from the closest hix site by DNA looping (Johnson and Simon, 1985; Kahmann et al., 1985).
evidence: This describes the native configuration and is supported by citations.

claim: The enhancer can efficiently activate DNA inversion many kb away from the closest hix site by DNA looping.
source: Whereas the hin enhancer is normally positioned about 100 bp from one of the hix sites, it can efficiently activate DNA inversion many kb away from the closest hix site by DNA looping (Johnson and Simon, 1985; Kahmann et al., 1985).
evidence: This describes the flexibility of enhancer positioning and is supported by citations.

claim: Hin dimers bound to each hix site are remodeled within the invertasome into a chemically-active tetramer that is also competent for subunit rotation.
source: Hin dimers bound to each hix site are remodeled within the invertasome into a chemically-active tetramer that is also competent for subunit rotation.
evidence: This describes the conformational changes that occur during invertasome assembly.

claim: Crystal structure snapshots of several serine recombinases highlight the large conformational changes required for formation of the tetramer and reveal a flat and hydrophobic interface between rotating subunit pairs.
source: Crystal structure snapshots of several serine recombinases highlight the large conformational changes required for formation of the tetramer and reveal a flat and hydrophobic interface between rotating subunit pairs (Yang and Steitz, 1995; Li et al., 2005; Kamtekar et al., 2006; Yuan et al., 2008; Keenholtz et al., 2011; Ritacco et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes structural features revealed by crystal structures and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Formation of the supercoiling-dependent invertasome intermediate containing the Fis/enhancer element is the critical regulatory step in the Hin-catalyzed recombination reaction.
source: Formation of the supercoiling-dependent invertasome intermediate containing the Fis/enhancer element is the critical regulatory step in the Hin-catalyzed recombination reaction.
evidence: This describes the importance of invertasome formation in regulation.

claim: The invertasome functions to ensure that intramolecular DNA inversion is the exclusive outcome of the reaction.
source: It functions to ensure that intramolecular DNA inversion is the exclusive outcome of the reaction, promotes the Hin conformational changes required for DNA chemistry and exchange, and limits most subunit rotation reactions to a single 180° step (Kanaar et al., 1990; Heichman et al., 1991; Moskowitz et al., 1991; Merickel and Johnson, 2004) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes a function of the invertasome and is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The invertasome promotes the Hin conformational changes required for DNA chemistry and exchange.
source: It functions to ensure that intramolecular DNA inversion is the exclusive outcome of the reaction, promotes the Hin conformational changes required for DNA chemistry and exchange, and limits most subunit rotation reactions to a single 180° step (Kanaar et al., 1990; Heichman et al., 1991; Moskowitz et al., 1991; Merickel and Johnson, 2004) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes a function of the invertasome and is supported by citations.

claim: The invertasome limits most subunit rotation reactions to a single 180° step.
source: It functions to ensure that intramolecular DNA inversion is the exclusive outcome of the reaction, promotes the Hin conformational changes required for DNA chemistry and exchange, and limits most subunit rotation reactions to a single 180° step (Kanaar et al., 1990; Heichman et al., 1991; Moskowitz et al., 1991; Merickel and Johnson, 2004) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes a function of the invertasome and is supported by citations.

claim: Wild-type Hin is chemically inactive without the Fis/enhancer system.
source: Whereas wild-type Hin is chemically inactive without the Fis/enhancer system, mutants that no longer require the Fis/enhancer element or DNA supercoiling have been isolated (Klippel et al., 1988; Sanders and Johnson, 2004; Heiss et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the requirement for the Fis/enhancer system and is supported by citations.

claim: Mutants that no longer require the Fis/enhancer element or DNA supercoiling have been isolated.
source: Whereas wild-type Hin is chemically inactive without the Fis/enhancer system, mutants that no longer require the Fis/enhancer element or DNA supercoiling have been isolated (Klippel et al., 1988; Sanders and Johnson, 2004; Heiss et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the existence of hyperactive mutants and is supported by citations.

claim: Hyperactive Hin mutants catalyze recombination promiscuously, being no longer restricted to promoting inversion between recombination sites on the same DNA molecule and no longer confined to a single round of subunit rotation.
source: These hyperactive mutants catalyze recombination promiscuously, being no longer restricted to promoting inversion between recombination sites on the same DNA molecule and no longer confined to a single round of subunit rotation.
evidence: This describes the properties of hyperactive mutants.

claim: Three residues on one of the mobile β-hairpin arms of the Fis dimer are required to activate Hin-catalyzed DNA inversion through direct contact with Hin.
source: Three residues on one of the mobile β-hairpin arms of the Fis dimer are required to activate Hin-catalyzed DNA inversion through direct contact with Hin (Figure 1B) (Koch et al., 1991; Osuna et al., 1991; Safo et al., 1997; Dhar et al., 2009a).
evidence: This describes previous findings about Fis-Hin interactions and is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Fis-Q21C exhibits efficient crosslinking with Hin beginning at 4.4 Å.
source: Fis-Q21C exhibits efficient crosslinking with Hin beginning at 4.4 Å, whereas Fis-Q19C exhibits less efficient crosslinking beginning at 7.3 Å.
evidence: This is supported by the crosslinking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fis-Q19C exhibits less efficient crosslinking beginning at 7.3 Å.
source: Fis-Q21C exhibits efficient crosslinking with Hin beginning at 4.4 Å, whereas Fis-Q19C exhibits less efficient crosslinking beginning at 7.3 Å.
evidence: This is supported by the crosslinking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hin-K51A and K158A exhibited reduced amounts of Fis-Hin-(32P-DNA) crosslinked products relative to Hin-wt.
source: Hin-K51A and K158A exhibited reduced amounts of Fis-Hin-(32P-DNA) crosslinked products relative to Hin-wt (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the crosslinking data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Hin-K146C at the N-terminus of helix 1 within the DBD generated ∼15% crosslinked Fis-Hin products.
source: Hin-K146C at the N-terminus of helix 1 within the DBD generated ∼15% crosslinked Fis-Hin products (Figure 2B,D), a level similar to that of wild-type Hin crosslinked to Fis-Q21C by AMAS.
evidence: This is supported by the BMOE crosslinking data shown in Figure 2B,D.

claim: Hin-H147C, Hin-E150C, and Hin-Q151C within the α-helix formed crosslinks with Fis-Q21C.
source: Hin-H147C, Hin-E150C, and Hin-Q151C within the α-helix formed crosslinks with Fis-Q21C, but H160C in the loop connecting to DBD helix 2 did not generate crosslinks.
evidence: This is supported by the crosslinking data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: H160C in the loop connecting to DBD helix 2 did not generate crosslinks with Fis-Q21C.
source: Hin-H147C, Hin-E150C, and Hin-Q151C within the α-helix formed crosslinks with Fis-Q21C, but H160C in the loop connecting to DBD helix 2 did not generate crosslinks.
evidence: This is supported by the crosslinking data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The 8 Å crosslinks between Fis-Q21C and five positions within helix 1 of the Hin DBD demonstrate that the Hin DBD is in close proximity to the Fis β-hairpin arms in the DNA-cleaved invertasome.
source: The 8 Å crosslinks between Fis-Q21C and five positions within helix 1 of the Hin DBD demonstrate that the Hin DBD is in close proximity to the Fis β-hairpin arms in the DNA-cleaved invertasome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the crosslinking data.

claim: Q151A, R154A, and L155A exhibited strong reductions of Fis-activated DNA inversion in vivo and in vitro.
source: Of the 11 solvent-exposed residues tested, Q151A, R154A, and L155A, exhibited strong reductions of Fis-activated DNA inversion in vivo and in vitro (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 1.

claim: Hin-L155A exhibits a >50-fold decrease of Fis-activated DNA inversion rates in vitro.
source: The most severe mutant, Hin-L155A, exhibits a >50-fold decrease of Fis-activated DNA inversion rates in vitro, comparable to the effects of the strongest Fis β-hairpin arm point mutations (Safo et al., 1997) (see also Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro inversion rate data in Table 1 and comparison to previous work.

claim: Hin-H107Y/L155A catalyze recombination in the absence of Fis at similar rates to Hin-H107Y.
source: In contrast, both Hin-H107Y and the double mutant Hin-H107Y/L155A catalyze recombination in the absence of Fis at similar rates.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Fis specifically interacts with Hin residues Arg154 and Leu155 and these contacts are required for DNA inversion catalyzed by wild-type Hin.
source: Taken together, we conclude that Fis specifically interacts with Hin residues Arg154 and Leu155 and that these contacts are required for DNA inversion catalyzed by wild-type Hin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis and rescue experiments.

claim: Fis contacts the DBDs of only the bottom two Hin subunits within the cleaved invertasome.
source: These crosslinking results demonstrate that Fis contacts the DBDs of only the bottom two Hin subunits within the cleaved invertasome as drawn in Figure 3A.
evidence: This is supported by the site-specific crosslinking data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Fis-Hin crosslinks only occurred with Hin subunits bound to hix1L and hix2R.
source: Fis-Hin crosslinks were only observed when Hin was bound to hix1L or to hix2R; no Fis-Hin crosslinks formed at hix1R or hix2L.
evidence: This is supported by the crosslinking data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Fis-activated DNA inversion rates of Hin-R47A, R48A, and K51A are moderately decreased with R47A and K51A exhibiting about threefold reductions in vitro.
source: Fis-activated DNA inversion rates of Hin-R47A, R48A, and K51A are moderately decreased with R47A and K51A exhibiting about threefold reductions in vitro (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the inversion rate data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The combinations of K47A/R48A and R48A/K51A severely impair Fis-activated Hin inversion both in vivo and in vitro.
source: However, the combinations of K47A/R48A and R48A/K51A severely impair Fis-activated Hin inversion both in vivo and in vitro (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Hin-R48A/K51A/H107Y promotes Fis-independent inversion at rates that are indistinguishable from the single H107Y mutant.
source: Hin-R48A/K51A/H107Y promotes Fis-independent inversion at rates that are indistinguishable from the single H107Y mutant (Figure 4C), demonstrating that these mutations are not disturbing Hin catalytic properties.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Basic residues in the Hin helix-B region function in the Fis/enhancer-dependent activation step of the Hin-catalyzed DNA inversion reaction.
source: We conclude that basic residues in the Hin helix-B region function in the Fis/enhancer-dependent activation step of the Hin-catalyzed DNA inversion reaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis and rescue experiments.

claim: Wild-type Hin efficiently forms knots only on pMS634 containing the long spacer.
source: Hin-wt efficiently forms knots only on pMS634 containing the long spacer, whereas Hin-R48A and K51A are insensitive to spacer length, reflecting an unstable interaction with the enhancer.
evidence: This is supported by the knotting data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Hin-R48A and K51A are insensitive to spacer length, reflecting an unstable interaction with the enhancer.
source: Hin-wt efficiently forms knots only on pMS634 containing the long spacer, whereas Hin-R48A and K51A are insensitive to spacer length, reflecting an unstable interaction with the enhancer.
evidence: This is supported by the knotting data shown in Figure 4E and interpreted as evidence for unstable enhancer interaction.

claim: Hin-N54C-FeBABE generated two prominent scission sites within the center of the enhancer segment.
source: Hin-N54C-FeBABE, and to a lesser extent Hin-Y52C-FeBABE, generated two prominent scission sites within the center of the enhancer segment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the FeBABE scission data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The scission sites by Hin-N54C-FeBABE are located between the Fis dimer binding sites.
source: These are located between the Fis dimer binding sites, as demarked by DNA scission induced by Fis-N98C coupled with FeBABE (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B); DNA scission by chemical nucleases coupled to Fis residue 98 has been used previously to map Fis binding site locations (Pan et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by the FeBABE scission data and comparison to Fis-N98C-FeBABE scission sites.

claim: When most of the DNA between the two Fis binding sites is replaced by non-native sequence (pRJ765), Hin inversion rates are reduced about fivefold.
source: When most of the DNA between the two Fis binding sites is replaced by non-native sequence (pRJ765, Figure 5D), Hin inversion rates are reduced about fivefold (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by the inversion rate data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: When only the two A/T-rich segments identified to be in proximity to the Hin helix-B region by the FeBABE experiments are replaced by G/C-rich sequences (pRJ2943), Hin inversion rates are reduced 2.5-fold.
source: When only the two A/T-rich segments identified to be in proximity to the Hin helix-B region by the FeBABE experiments are replaced by G/C-rich sequences (pRJ2943, Figure 5D), Hin inversion rates are reduced 2.5-fold (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by the inversion rate data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: There is a modest effect of sequence identity within the enhancer DNA segments that are contacted by the helix-B region of Hin.
source: We conclude that there is a modest effect of sequence identity within the enhancer DNA segments that are contacted by the helix-B region of Hin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the enhancer mutation data.

claim: Disulfide-linked Hin-M101C dimers bind normally to hix sites but are locked in an inactive conformation.
source: Disulfide-linked Hin-M101C dimers (Figure 6B) bind normally to hix sites but are locked in an inactive conformation (Figure 6C, lane 4) (Haykinson et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6C and a citation to previous work.

claim: Upon reduction of the disulfide bond and in the presence of Fis, Hin-M101C can proceed to generate DNA-cleaved invertasomes.
source: Upon reduction of the disulfide bond and in the presence of Fis, Hin-M101C can proceed to generate DNA-cleaved invertasomes (Figure 6C, lane 5) and ligated inversion products (Haykinson et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6C and a citation to previous work.

claim: Hin dimers that are covalently crosslinked with Fis on the enhancer can be remodeled into catalytically-active tetramers.
source: We conclude that Hin dimers that are covalently crosslinked with Fis on the enhancer can be remodeled into catalytically-active tetramers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the crosslinking experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Both the Fis-Hin crosslinked and uncrosslinked complexes were able to efficiently promote DNA ligation.
source: As recognized by the loss of the Hin serine-DNA linkage in the Fis-Hin-(32P-DNA) and Hin-(32P-DNA) bands, both the Fis-Hin crosslinked (Figure 6F, lanes 3, 4 and 5, 6) and uncrosslinked (lanes 1, 2) complexes were able to efficiently promote DNA ligation.
evidence: This is supported by the ligation data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Ligation can efficiently occur when Hin is covalently linked to Fis.
source: We conclude that ligation can efficiently occur when Hin is covalently linked to Fis, reinforcing earlier topological data indicating that the enhancer normally remains associated with the Hin complex throughout the reaction (Heichman et al., 1991; Merickel and Johnson, 2004; Dhar et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ligation data and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The hin enhancer contains two Fis dimer binding sites separated by 47 bp between their centers.
source: The hin enhancer contains two Fis dimer binding sites separated by 47 bp between their centers (Figure 5D) (Johnson and Simon, 1985; Bruist et al., 1987; Johnson et al., 1987).
evidence: This describes the structure of the enhancer and is supported by citations.

claim: A structural model of the Fis-bound enhancer results in an S-shaped DNA structure due to Fis-induced bending.
source: A structural model of the Fis-bound enhancer ('Materials and methods') results in an S-shaped DNA structure due to Fis-induced bending (see Figure 7F; Video 1).
evidence: This describes the modeled structure of the Fis-bound enhancer.

claim: Previous helical phasing experiments provide strong evidence that the shape of the enhancer segment is critical for function.
source: Previous helical phasing experiments provide strong evidence that the shape of the enhancer segment is critical for function (Johnson et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Extensive site-directed crosslinking data supports the validity of the Hin tetramer model for the DNA-cleaved Hin synaptic complex.
source: Extensive site-directed crosslinking data supports the validity of this model for the DNA-cleaved Hin synaptic complex, which is in a structure competent for DNA exchange by subunit rotation (Li et al., 2005; Dhar et al., 2009a, 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous crosslinking studies.

claim: The primary interaction surface between Fis and Hin is composed of Val16 and Val22 on Fis and Leu155 on Hin together with Asp20 on Fis and Arg154 on Hin.
source: Our data are consistent with the primary interaction surface between these proteins being composed of Val16 and Val22 on Fis and Leu155 on Hin together with Asp20 on Fis and Arg154 on Hin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis data and supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hin residues Arg154, Leu155, and Gln151 are conserved among Fis/enhancer-dependent DNA invertases, but not the related resolvases.
source: Significantly, Hin residues Arg154, Leu155, and Gln151, which also may contribute to the Fis contact patch, are conserved among Fis/enhancer-dependent DNA invertases, but not the related resolvases (Figure 8A), further supporting the function of these residues in the Fis-activation step.
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The basic character of key residues within the helix-B region is uniquely conserved among the DNA invertase subclass of serine recombinases.
source: The basic character of key residues within the helix-B region is also uniquely conserved among the DNA invertase subclass of serine recombinases (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Of the 15 DNA invertases aligned, residue 47 is always a lysine, and residues 48 and 51 are equally represented by lysine and arginine.
source: Of the 15 DNA invertases we have aligned, residue 47 is always a lysine, and residues 48 and 51 are equally represented by lysine and arginine, suggesting they are not involved in base-specific interactions.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis and suggests a functional interpretation.

claim: Members of the resolvase or integrase subclasses of serine recombinases tend to not have lysines and arginines at the same positions as DNA invertases.
source: Members of the resolvase or integrase subclasses of serine recombinases, which are not regulated by a Fis/enhancer system, tend to not have lysines and arginines at the same positions, and the electrostatic surface over this region in the resolvase tetramer is much less basic (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both γδ/Tn3 and Sin resolvases contain nearby regulatory residues that mediate critical protein-protein contacts during assembly of their respective synaptic complexes.
source: However, as discussed further below, both γδ/Tn3 and Sin resolvases contain nearby regulatory residues that mediate critical protein-protein contacts during assembly of their respective synaptic complexes (Hughes et al., 1990; Murley and Grindley, 1998; Burke et al., 2004; Mouw et al., 2008; Olorunniji et al., 2008; Rowland et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on resolvases.

claim: The Fis/enhancer system initially functions to promote synapsis and remodeling of Hin dimers into the active tetramer.
source: However, the Fis/enhancer system initially functions much earlier in the pathway to promote synapsis and remodeling of Hin dimers into the active tetramer, as wild-type Hin is unable to form active tetramers without the Fis/enhancer element (Dhar et al., 2004; Sanders and Johnson, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Fis is able to productively contact inactive Hin dimers.
source: We demonstrate here that Fis is able to productively contact inactive Hin dimers and that Hin dimers covalently crosslinked to Fis can transition into an active tetramer competent for DNA cleavage (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the crosslinking data shown in Figure 6A–D.

claim: Conformational energy from DNA supercoiling appears essential to promote synapsis.
source: As Fis-Hin interactions have not been observed by standard solution assays, conformational energy from DNA supercoiling appears essential to promote synapsis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of detectable Fis-Hin interactions in solution.

claim: A single clockwise rotation of subunits together with their linked DNA strands will result in inversion of the DNA between the hix sites with an accompanying loss of four supercoils.
source: A single clockwise rotation of subunits together with their linked DNA strands will result in inversion of the DNA between the hix sites with an accompanying loss of four supercoils, as shown for Hin- and Gin-mediated DNA inversion (Kanaar et al., 1988; Merickel and Johnson, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on DNA topology.

claim: When the distance between a hix site and the enhancer is short, the small loop will inhibit additional subunit rotations because of torsional strain generated from multiple DNA windings.
source: When the distance between a hix site and the enhancer is short, as in the native configuration in the Salmonella chromosome (∼100 bp between hixL and the proximal Fis binding site), the small loop will inhibit additional subunit rotations because of torsional strain generated from multiple DNA windings (illustrated in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an inference based on topological considerations and illustrated in Figure 4D.

claim: Additional rotations can occur under conditions where the loop is expanded by release of the Fis/enhancer from the Hin tetramer during the reaction or with substrates containing long segments of DNA between hixL and the enhancer.
source: However, additional rotations can occur under conditions where the loop is expanded by release of the Fis/enhancer from the Hin tetramer during the reaction or with substrates containing long segments of DNA between hixL and the enhancer.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of processive recombination.

claim: The structures of the resulting knotted DNA products are fully consistent with DNA exchange initiating within the invertasome model.
source: The structures of the resulting knotted DNA products are fully consistent with DNA exchange initiating within our invertasome model (Kanaar et al., 1990; Heichman et al., 1991; Crisona et al., 1994; Merickel and Johnson, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous topological studies.

claim: The multiple connections stabilizing the Hin tetramer onto the Fis/enhancer element function to restrict processive subunit exchanges.
source: Thus, the multiple connections stabilizing the Hin tetramer onto the Fis/enhancer element function to restrict processive subunit exchanges.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the knotting data and topological considerations.

claim: The invertasome normally remains intact over the course of the entire reaction.
source: We experimentally demonstrate in this work that the final chemical step in the reaction, Hin-catalyzed DNA ligation, can efficiently occur when Fis and Hin remain physically connected (Figure 6F), implying that the invertasome normally remains intact over the course of the entire reaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ligation data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In the Sin-catalyzed deletion reaction, synapsis is initiated by an interaction between regulatory dimers bound to each recombination site via residues in their DBD helix 1.
source: In the Sin-catalyzed deletion reaction, synapsis is initiated by an interaction between regulatory dimers bound to each recombination site via residues in their DBD helix 1 (Figure 8A) (Mouw et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on Sin.

claim: The DBD interaction by the Sin regulatory dimers is dispensable in the context of hyperactive mutants that promote recombination in the absence of the regulatory sub-sites.
source: As with Hin, the DBD interaction by the Sin regulatory dimers is dispensable in the context of hyperactive mutants that promote recombination in the absence of the regulatory sub-sites.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work on Sin.

claim: For Sin, a second protein interface required for recombination involves residues Phe52 and Arg54 that are located immediately adjacent to helix-B.
source: A second protein interface required for recombination by Sin, as well as the γδ/Tn3 resolvases, occurs between regulatory and catalytic subunits and can be related to the helix-B—enhancer DNA interface in the Hin invertasome. For Sin this interaction involves residues Phe52 and Arg54 that are located immediately adjacent to helix-B (Figure 8B) (Mouw et al., 2008; Rowland et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on Sin.

claim: For γδ/Tn3 resolvases a cluster of residues (Arg2, Arg32, Lys54, and Glu56) comprising the so-called 2–3′ interface between regulatory and catalytic dimers is important for assembly of the active synaptosome.
source: For γδ/Tn3 resolvases a cluster of residues (Arg2, Arg32, Lys54, and Glu56; Figure 8B) comprising the so-called 2–3′ interface between regulatory and catalytic dimers is important for assembly of the active synaptosome (Hughes et al., 1990; Murley and Grindley, 1998; Burke et al., 2004; Olorunniji et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on resolvases.

claim: The interaction between regulatory and catalytic subunits in the resolvase reactions is dispensable in the context of strong hyperactive mutants that promote indiscriminant recombination.
source: Like Hin, the interaction between regulatory and catalytic subunits in the resolvase reactions is dispensable in the context of strong hyperactive mutants that promote indiscriminant recombination (Burke et al., 2004; Olorunniji et al., 2008; Rowland et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on resolvases.

claim: Protein-protein or DNA-protein forces acting on the helix-B region may not only stabilize the active recombination complex but promote remodeling of this subfamily of serine recombinases into their active tetrameric conformation.
source: Taken together, the Hin, Sin, and γδ/Tn3 results imply that protein-protein or DNA-protein forces acting on this region of the catalytic domain may not only stabilize the active recombination complex but promote remodeling of this subfamily of serine recombinases into their active tetrameric conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the results across different serine recombinases.
